支聯會被指煽動顛覆案，不認罪的李卓人和鄒幸彤歷經 24 日審訊，8 月 21 日迎來裁決。《集誌社》回顧庭上令人印象深刻的畫面與對答，讓讀者重溫兩人作供重點。1997 年六四，維園。身穿「不想回憶！未敢忘記！」黑色上衣的李卓人，拿着咪高峰以英文宣讀：「有人說，這是我們支持民主運動的最後一次燭光集會，也是中國民主的最後一夜。親愛的同胞，這絕對不正確，主權移交後，支聯會將繼續每年在維園舉辦燭光集會⋯⋯」當時 40 歲的李卓人，頭髮烏黑、臉頰圓潤。將近 30 年後，已屆 68 歲、一頭白髮的李卓人，坐在被告欄，望着螢幕中的自己，握拳放在鼻前，輕輕抿嘴，以手指拭淚。這名支聯會元老被控煽動顛覆國家政權，不認罪，就六四經歷和支聯會理念出庭作證。他在播放昔日六四集會片段時流淚、憶起基層的慘況時哽咽，亦不諱言《國安法》後仍堅持五大綱領，全因「基於對人民嘅愛」。支聯會案相關報道 支聯會案．庭審筆記｜鄒幸彤的「意圖」 支聯會案｜歷 24 日審訊　8.21 裁決　整合九項案情關鍵及法律爭議

Lee Cheuk-yan was jailed in April 2021 over the August 18 unauthorised assembly case, and by the time of the verdict had been deprived of his liberty for more than five years and four months.

Born into Comfort, Raised in a China of Suffering, Determined to Take Responsibility

On the 13th day of the trial, Lee Cheuk-yan, with a shock of white hair and dressed in a dark grey long-sleeved shirt and black padded vest, stepped into the witness box. He smiled and nodded to the public gallery, took a Catholic oath, and began to give evidence.

Lee Cheuk-yan's more than 40 years of labour activism and political career began during his university days. He enrolled in the civil engineering department of the University of Hong Kong in 1975. On campus he encountered the " recognise China, engage with society" movement, and came to know Wei Jingsheng's call for a "fifth modernisation" – democracy. Coming from a comfortable family, he also took part in the student hostel association and threw himself into grassroots movements, experiences that left a deep impression on him.

As he recalled visiting boat-dwellers and a child who had drowned, his voice broke, and the scene from over 40 years ago seemed to flash before his eyes. He said his generation was a product of its time, that being born in a suffering China meant bearing a responsibility, and after graduation he had decided not to practise civil engineering, wanting instead to "do something" for Hong Kong society and for China.

"Against that background, I began my lifelong …," he smiled. "I'd never have thought I'd be doing it for a whole lifetime." His leading counsel, Simon Shum, asked: "A lifetime of what?" Lee replied: "A lifetime of labour activism, and of caring about democracy in China."

Lee Cheuk-yan told the court that the "recognise China, engage with society"思潮 of his university years had shaped him, and from then on he devoted himself to grassroots concerns, trade unions and the democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

Baptised by June Fourth – Supporting the Pro-Democracy Movement Becomes a Lifelong Commitment

From then on, Lee Cheuk-yan devoted himself to labour activism while keeping a close eye on China's pro-democracy movement. When the 1989 pro-democracy movement erupted, the 32-year-old was working as an officer at the Hong Kong Christian Industrial Committee. He recalled that after Hu Yaobang's death in April 1989, students gathered in Tiananmen Square to express their grievances against corruption and official profiteering, and Hong Kong people marched to the Xinhua News Agency and held a sit-in in solidarity; he was there in the capacity of marshal of the march.

After the Beijing students began their hunger strike, more than a million people in Hong Kong took to the streets in two huge marches in solidarity, and on 27 May a "Democratic Songs Dedicated to China"concert was held at the Happy Valley racecourse, raising about HK$12 million. On 21 May, Szeto Wah announced the formation of the Hong Kong Alliance, and just over a week later Lee Cheuk-yan travelled to Beijing with other Alliance representatives and a donation of HK$1 million.

Lee Cheuk-yan was detained after the Tiananmen crackdown; he said it was Hong Kong citizens' calls for his release that saved him and steeled his resolve to continue supporting China's pro-democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

In Tiananmen Square he saw students, workers and intellectuals fighting to have the 26 April editorial – which had branded the movement a "disturbance" – retracted: "They wanted to tell the authorities … that we are patriots, we just want our country to do well – that sense of patriotism was very strong at the time." Late on the night of 3 June, while he was in the workers' tent, he was suddenly told to leave: "They said the army was coming in, that they were going out to block the troops." Back at the hotel he stayed awake all night, "looking outside, hearing the gunfire, watching Tiananmen Square …". He fell silent for a moment. "Around four o'clock … the lights went out."

After June Fourth, Lee Cheuk-yan and the supporters, students and journalists evacuated, but on the chartered flight home he was asked to disembark by public security officers. He was held for two days; his donation was confiscated and he was made to sign a statement of repentance before being allowed to return to Hong Kong.

Having witnessed in Tiananmen Square the dead and wounded being driven past on tricycle carts along Chang'an Avenue, and later heard the accounts of the massacre, he described June Fourth as another baptism. "Beijing citizens told us at the time to tell the whole world what we had seen"; while he was being held, Hong Kong people marched to the Governor's House and the Xinhua News Agency demanding his release – "it was Hong Kong people who saved me." After returning, he resolved to keep supporting China's pro-democracy movement, to push China and Hong Kong towards democracy: "I felt an even greater sense of responsibility; it became the commitment of my life."

After his detention, Lee Cheuk-yan had his donation confiscated and was made to sign a statement of repentance before being allowed to return to Hong Kong. Signing that statement became the lifelong regret he still carries. (Facebook photo)

Insisting on the Five Core Demands – Autocracy and Democracy Are Antithetical

The full name of the Alliance – the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China – was officially established in early June 1989, and Lee Cheuk-yan was among its first standing committee members. He explained that the organisation's remit was to support movements that originated inside the country; it welcomed anyone of like mind, including pro-Beijing groups; it had always been peaceful and non-violent; and prior to 2020 its annual June Fourth vigils had each received a letter of no objection from the police.

The Alliance's much-defended "five core demands" had, Lee said, never changed and were like "links in a chain": first, the release of those imprisoned; then, recognition that the movement was a patriotic democratic movement and that the massacre and crackdown were wrong, and demands to hold those responsible to account; and finally, carrying forward the demands of the 1989 movement – an end to one-party dictatorship, the enjoyment by the people of freedoms of speech, association and the press, and the building of civil society, so that there would be a basis to discuss democracy and the system best suited to China. He explained that dictatorship concentrated executive, legislative and judicial power to suppress and punish the people for speaking out, and was antithetical to democracy; without ending dictatorship, building a democratic China would be "simply impossible."

Lee stressed that the Alliance's role was one of support; it had never discussed which system China should adopt – they had not got that far: "If China has no freedom, if the people have no freedom, there is nothing to discuss." He also disagreed that "end one-party dictatorship" was the same as "end the leadership of the Communist Party": "Whether the Communist Party leads or not is not for us to say – that is for the people to decide."

The Alliance was officially founded in early June 1989; Lee Cheuk-yan (first right) was also a member of its first standing committee. (File photo)

Relaxed and Smiling as He Faced the Prosecution's Questions

While giving evidence, Lee Cheuk-yan was visibly at ease, his tone calm – much as he had addressed the media countless times before. Every question was met with a fluent, direct, sometimes even faintly humorous reply.

When the prosecution asked whether he did not wish the Communist Party to continue to rule, he smiled and spread his hands: "That's not for me to agree or disagree with – that is for the people to decide." When the prosecution suggested he believed that reform within the Party could not lead to the end of one-party dictatorship, he disagreed with a light laugh: "Don't pigeonhole the Communist Party like that," prompting laughter in the public gallery.

Asked by the judge whether he had been following the 2018 constitutional amendments, he laughed: "Frankly, no – I don't think the Communist Party's leadership depends on me, so why would I bother (follow it)?" He added: "I did notice they had wedged in 'leadership of the Communist Party'; my reaction at the time was, do they really need to? Everyone knows that." As to whether he wanted more people to put "end one-party dictatorship" into practice, he said with a smile that the question was a false one: "We would never call on people to take action to end one-party dictatorship – we would never phrase it that way."

In 2018 the constitutional amendments removed the two-term limit on the presidency. The prosecution alleged that the Alliance's demand to "end one-party dictatorship" was the same as ending the Communist Party's leadership, and was therefore an unconstitutional means.

"In My Heart There Is No Hostility, Only Love"

The prosecution twice suggested in court that Lee Cheuk-yan harboured hostility towards the Communist Party. The first time, Assistant Director of Public Prosecutions Winnie Lai-yee questioned whether he bore "extreme hostility" towards CCP rule. Lee shook his head and said: "Disagree." Lai-yee rephrased, asking whether there was "at least some hostility". Lee replied: "In my heart there is no hostility, only love. My motivation is love for the people; I hope the Communist Party will reform so that the people can enjoy the rights and happiness that are rightfully theirs."

On the second occasion, Lai-yee suggested that by constantly advocating "end one-party dictatorship", Lee was trying to instil in more people hostility towards the Communist Party. He denied this again, stressing more emphatically that what he wanted was for the public to have expectations of the Communist Party – for it to respect democracy and human rights. "You couldn't really call that hostility."

Lai-yee had put to Lee Cheuk-yan a string of questions about his views on the CCP. "Do you agree that the Alliance and you personally have always regarded the Chinese Communist Party as an authoritarian regime?" Lee tilted his head, thought for a few seconds, then answered: "Before '49 it wasn't authoritarian; after the founding of the country it has been." He then agreed, one by one, with the prosecution's other characterisations – that the Alliance considered the CCP "stifled the voices of the people, especially dissenting voices", "strangled democracy", "used the state apparatus to suppress the people", "violated human rights", "held elections in which the people had no real participation", and that "the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference is a rubber stamp".

"So do you agree that the Alliance believed the Chinese Communist Party, in governing the country, was in practice operating a one-party dictatorship?" "I agree, but it shouldn't be a one-party dictatorship," said Lee.

Lee Cheuk-yan denied harbouring hostility towards the CCP, saying: "In my heart there is no hostility, only love."

"Of Course I Am Absolutely Patriotic"

After Lee rejected the suggestion that he bore hostility towards CCP rule, the prosecution reframed it, suggesting he was "dissatisfied" with CCP rule and considered it "not good for the country". Lee said he believed in "praising what is right and condemning what is wrong"; there were policies he welcomed and others he did not, and his biggest grievance was that "the people have no voice and no basic rights". He also openly acknowledged that he had learned about organising trade unions from the Communist Party itself: "When I was young I genuinely admired the Communist Party."

Pressed repeatedly by the prosecution, he added: "It is doing the country no good, but we hope it will do better by the country and the people." He stressed again: "I want it to do well." Judge Andrew Chan asked whether he meant the Communist Party. Lee replied: "Yes, I want the Communist Party to do well."

Patriotism is not the same as loving the Party – that, perhaps, is one way into understanding what the Alliance stood for. In its opening, the prosecution cited a 2012 protest at which Lee was alleged to have said: "We are absolutely patriotic, but if we truly love our country we must end one-party dictatorship – that is what real patriotism means."

Lee's own barrister, in his final questions, asked him: the Alliance's full name contains the word "patriotic" – so did he love his country?

"I think from the moment I set foot in university, I already felt that a suffering China must have a future. Even then I wanted the country to grow strong, democratic and free; even then I resolved to work towards a better future for the people. Of course I am absolutely patriotic."

Asked whether he loved his country, Lee Cheuk-yan said he was "absolutely patriotic", adding that since his university days he had wanted the country to become prosperous, democratic and free. (File photo)
